title: The Shout-Out Trap
author: Dr Dario Emanuele
summary: Dario Emanuele examines the "Bright Spots" or "Shout Outs" section common at the top of school staff bulletins, conceding it is a genuinely good initiative for morale before identifying a subtle way it backfires. His move is an analogy from the classroom: just as constantly praising the same few students leaves the quieter majority feeling unnoticed and demotivated, repeatedly naming the same staff members creates the impression that leadership has favourites. He calls this the Shout-Out Trap, where a positivity initiative becomes a recurring micro-negative for most of the staff. The fix he proposes is for leaders to do what they ask teachers to do with students: keep a praise register of all teaching and non-teaching staff and rotate recognition so no one is praised twice before everyone has been named once. He adds that leaders should deliberately plan observations of staff not recently praised and seek out long-running, unglamorous commitments, on the assumption that for every excellent practice seen, several go unseen.
points: Emanuele transfers a classroom truth to staff leadership: praising the same small group demotivates the unseen majority and damages perceptions of fairness, whether the group is students or colleagues.
The practical tool is a Staff Markbook: a spreadsheet of all teaching and non-teaching staff where every bulletin shout-out is logged, with no repeat praise until every name has been marked.

He anticipates the objection that teachers are professionals who do not need praise, answering that the point is not coping but removing a repeated micro-negative that erodes team fidelity over years.
Leaders should assume that for every excellent practice they observe, at least five others went unseen, and so plan drop-ins on staff who have not been recognised recently.
Recognition should reach long-term, low-visibility commitments, such as a five-year lunchtime band or a steady homework club, not only whoever launches the newest initiative.
quotes: This dedicated space allows the leadership team to publicly acknowledge colleagues by name for great accomplishments, impressive achievements, or excellent practice observed in lessons. It spreads positive vibes, boosts morale, and encourages colleagues to connect and celebrate good work.
This is the Shout-Out Trap. A great initiative designed to boost positivity ends up becoming a micro-negative vibe for the majority who are consistently left out.

How can we ensure the shout-out initiative does not backfire? The solution is simple: Leadership members must do exactly what they expect their amazing staff to do with their students: Track and rotate praise.

I know what you’re thinking: Teachers are professionals, not children; they should be able to cope without praise. And you’re right, they can. But this isn’t about coping; it’s about eliminating a micro-negative vibe that, when repeated regularly over years, erodes team fidelity and energy.
It’s easy to praise the person who starts the new, shiny initiative. But what about the colleague who has run the Year 11 lunch break music band for five years straight?

A strong leadership team never leaves anyone behind. By applying the same principles of equity, visibility, and conscious rotation that we preach in the classroom, we can ensure the school bulletin remains a force for genuine, widespread positivity.
